item.title: It’s Time to Settle With Russia
item.description: In October, U.S. President Donald Trump sold his eleventh-hour deal to secure diesel from Russian President Vladimir Putin—pausing sanctions that his own administration had imposed—as a boon for the negotiations to end the war in Ukraine. item.title: CISA Adds Two Known Exploited Vulnerabilities to Catalog
item.description:
CISA has added two new vulnerabilities to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) Catalog, based on evidence of active exploitation.

  • CVE-2026-133968 Project MONAI MONAI Label Path Traversal Vulnerability

  •  CVE-2026-134624 N-able Mail Assure (SpamExperts) Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF) Vulnerability

These types of vulnerabilities are a frequent attack vector for malicious cyber actors and pose significant risks to the federal enterprise.

Binding Operational Directive (BOD) 26-04: Prioritizing Security Updates Based on Risk establishes vulnerability management requirements for Federal Civilian Executive Branch (FCEB) agencies. BOD 26-04 reinforces the importance of the KEV Catalog and requires federal agencies to prioritize rapid remediation of high-risk vulnerabilities, specifically those identified by Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVEs) listed in CISA’s KEV Catalog on publicly exposed assets that grant total control of the asset post-exploitation, while deferring action for lower-risk vulnerabilities. BOD 26-04 further establishes basic expectations for when agencies must check whether threat actors compromised the system before the patch was applied.

While BOD 26-04 applies only to FCEB agencies, CISA encourages all organizations to adopt risk-based vulnerability management and prioritize remediation of KEV Catalog vulnerabilities. CISA will continue to add vulnerabilities to the catalog that meet the specified criteria.

Aware of an exploited vulnerability not currently listed in the KEV Catalog? Submit it for potential addition through CISA’s KEV Nomination Form. Potential KEV additions must have a CVE ID, evidence of exploitation, and clear mitigation guidance.

item.description:

Summary

Successful exploitation of this vulnerability could allow attackers to corrupt application memory and cause instability or a crash, potentially leading to arbitrary code execution, if a user is convinced to open a malicious file.

  • Company Headquarters Location: United States

Vulnerabilities

CVE-2026-127280
C-More EA9 Programming Software V6.80 does not adequately validate data read from a project file before using it in heap memory operations. A crafted file causes a heap buffer overrun during file open, resulting in heap corruption and instability within the application. An attacker can exploit this vulnerability by convincing a user to open a malicious project file delivered through common distribution channels such as email, file sharing, or removable media.

AutomationDirect C-More EA9 Programming Software <=V6.80

Product Status: known_affected

Remediations

Vendor fix
Update C-More EA9 Programming Software to V6.81: https://www.automationdirect.com/support/software-downloads

Mitigation
If you cannot update to the latest software or firmware version right away, apply the following compensating controls to reduce risk until the update can be performed. These measures are temporary and do not replace the update, which remains the primary and recommended remediation. Apply these controls as appropriate based on the vulnerability, assessed risk, operational requirements, and characteristics of your environment. Implement changes under your established management-of-change process. Before implementing isolation, access-control, or network-configuration changes, evaluate potential impacts to safety, availability, and essential operational functions. • Isolate affected engineering workstations and OT systems from external and nonessential networks, including the internet and corporate IT networks, where operationally feasible. • Disable or tightly restrict vendor, contractor, and other remote access to the affected OT environment until the vulnerability can be remediated. Where remote access is operationally required, use a hardened jump host, enforce multi-factor authentication, apply least-privilege access, and limit access to authorized, time-bound sessions. • Use trusted, dedicated OT networks for device communication. Where practicable and appropriate to the assessed risk, use dedicated or physically separated infrastructure for higher-criticality systems. Where logical segmentation is used, ensure segmentation controls are appropriately configured, secured, and monitored. • Restrict both physical and logical access to affected systems to authorized personnel only. Apply least-privilege principles to administrative, engineering, maintenance, and service access. • Configure application allowlisting, where supported, so that only trusted and pre-approved applications are permitted to execute. Block unauthorized software. • Use appropriate antivirus or endpoint detection and response (EDR) tools where supported and compatible with the affected system. Configure host-based and network firewalls to permit only required communications. • Disable unnecessary services, ports, protocols, and communication pathways associated with the affected systems. Where a service or protocol cannot be disabled for operational reasons, restrict access to trusted systems and authorized users wherever possible. • Enable and regularly review available system, security, and network logs to identify suspicious or unauthorized activity. Where appropriate, monitor communications to and from affected systems for unexpected connections or changes in network behavior. • Maintain secure, tested, and preferably offline backups of PLC programs, device configurations, engineering workstation configurations, and other information necessary to restore operations. Periodically verify that backups can be successfully restored. • Verify that critical OT functions can continue operating without unnecessary dependencies on external networks, cloud services, remote-access services, corporate IT services, or other nonessential systems. • If removable media is required to transfer files into an isolated or restricted environment, use controlled and trusted media and scan it for malicious content before use. • Continuously evaluate the risks associated with operating vulnerable or outdated firmware or software. Adjust compensating controls as the threat environment, operational requirements, or available vulnerability information changes. These compensating controls are intended to reduce exposure while remediation is pending. Organizations should prioritize applying the vendor-provided update as soon as it can be safely tested and deployed within the operational environment.

Recommended Practices

CISA recommends users take defensive measures to minimize the risk of exploitation of these vulnerabilities.

  • Minimize network exposure for all control system devices and/or systems, ensuring they are not accessible from the internet.
  • Locate control system networks and remote devices behind firewalls and isolating them from business networks.
  • When remote access is required, use more secure methods, such as Virtual Private Networks (VPNs), recognizing VPNs may have vulnerabilities and should be updated to the most current version available. Also recognize VPN is only as secure as the connected devices.

CISA reminds organizations to perform proper impact analysis and risk assessment prior to deploying defensive measures.

CISA also provides a section for control systems security recommended practices on the ICS webpage on cisa.gov/ics. Several CISA products detailing cyber defense best practices are available for reading and download, including Improving Industrial Control Systems Cybersecurity with Defense-in-Depth Strategies.

CISA encourages organizations to implement recommended cybersecurity strategies for proactive defense of ICS assets.

Additional mitigation guidance and recommended practices are publicly available on the ICS webpage at cisa.gov/ics in the technical information paper, ICS-TIP-12-146-01B--Targeted Cyber Intrusion Detection and Mitigation Strategies.

Organizations observing suspected malicious activity should follow established internal procedures and report findings to CISA for tracking and correlation against other incidents.

CISA also recommends users take the following measures to protect themselves from social engineering attacks:

  • Do not click web links or open attachments in unsolicited email messages.
  • Refer to Recognizing and Avoiding Email Scams for more information on avoiding email scams.
  • Refer to Avoiding Social Engineering and Phishing Attacks for more information on social engineering attacks.

item.title: CISA Adds Three Known Exploited Vulnerabilities to Catalog
item.description:
CISA has added three new vulnerabilities to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) Catalog, based on evidence of active exploitation.

  • CVE-2026-131914 Idunno AntiCsrf Deserialization of Untrusted Data Vulnerability 

  • CVE-2026-132165 Drupal Core Remote Code Execution Vulnerability 

  • CVE-2026-132224 Optimizely Web Experimentation External Control of Critical State Data Vulnerability 

These types of vulnerabilities are a frequent attack vector for malicious cyber actors and pose significant risks to the federal enterprise.

Binding Operational Directive (BOD) 26-04: Prioritizing Security Updates Based on Risk establishes vulnerability management requirements for Federal Civilian Executive Branch (FCEB) agencies. BOD 26-04 reinforces the importance of the KEV Catalog and requires federal agencies to prioritize rapid remediation of high-risk vulnerabilities, specifically those identified by Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVEs) listed in CISA’s KEV Catalog on publicly exposed assets that grant total control of the asset post-exploitation, while deferring action for lower-risk vulnerabilities. BOD 26-04 further establishes basic expectations for when agencies must check whether threat actors compromised the system before the patch was applied.

While BOD 26-04 applies only to FCEB agencies, CISA encourages all organizations to adopt risk-based vulnerability management and prioritize remediation of KEV Catalog vulnerabilities. CISA will continue to add vulnerabilities to the catalog that meet the specified criteria.

Aware of an exploited vulnerability not currently listed in the KEV Catalog? Submit it for potential addition through CISA’s KEV Nomination Form. Potential KEV additions must have a CVE ID, evidence of exploitation, and clear mitigation guidance.

item.description:
Country: Somalia
Sources: Norwegian Refugee Council, SOS Children's Villages International

Please refer to the attached file.

Executive Summary

Between 29 August and 13 September 2026, intensified security operations and armed confrontations in parts of Lower Shabelle, including Basra, Alifow, Baqdaad and Areer Mooge, displaced more than 860 households (approximately 5,100 people, including about 3,640 children) towards Afgooye and surrounding communities, according to cluster/ABC reporting. An estimated 620 children are currently out of school.

SOS Children’s Villages Somalia conducted a field visit and community dialogue in four IDP locations in Lafoole (Waafi, Docol, Durdur and Takulo) to verify the presence of newly displaced families, understand education and protection needs, and identify potential FLER sites. The assessment identified 402 newly displaced households. Education is the most urgent gap: existing public schools are located approximately 1 km to more than 3 km from the settlements, and children who remain out of school face heightened risks of abuse, neglect, exploitation, child labour, family separation, early marriage and psychosocial distress.

Immediate FLER activation is therefore strongly justified. FLER will provide safe, structured learning, psychosocial support, play and life-skills activities, foundational learning and protection identification and referral, while creating a pathway into neighbouring schools. Docol and Durdur IDP Community Centres are the priority FLER locations, covering multiple surrounding IDP subcamps.

item.title: Kenya: Gender-based violence: a public health and human rights concern
item.description:
Country: Kenya
Source: World Health Organization

Nairobi— Married at the age of 14, Mparakoni Leabune from Samburu County in northern Kenya was the third wife in a polygamous union. “My husband used to beat me a lot," she says. "That is how I got this leg injury," she says pointing to severe swelling on her left leg. Despite countless medical interventions, Leabune has endured a long and painful road to recovery.
"My husband divorced me and now I live with my mother," she says.

Aside from enduring physical violence, Leabune is a survivor of early marriage, which is also considered a form of gender-based violence.

According to Kenya’s 2022 Demographic Health Survey, more than a third of women (34%) in Kenya have experienced physical violence since the age of 15 years, and 13% have experienced sexual violence in their lifetime. Nine out of 10 times, the perpetrator is a either a current or former husband or partner.

Furthermore, according to the 2025/2026 Kenya Mini-Demographic Heath Survey, technology- facilitated gender-based violence is on the rise: more than a quarter of women aged age 15–49 have ever experienced it from any perpetrator. Technology- facilitated gender-based violence includes acts such as online harassment, cyberbullying and online control to cause harm.
“Women are suffering silently because they cannot seek medical attention, not because of their own will, but because of the patriarchal society we live in," says Samson Esward Leerte, nurse and reproductive health coordinator for adolescents and young people in Samburu County.

The 2010 Constitution protects people in Kenya from harmful cultural practices and violence. Several laws have been enacted and most recently, the National Policy on Gender-based Violence and the National Policy for the Eradication of Female Genital Mutilation were adopted in 2019.

The country is taking steps to ramp up implementation of these laws.

In January 2025, President Williams Ruto established a technical working group on gender-based violence, including femicide. In November 2025, he heard its recommendations. They include several recommendations to curb femicide and female genital mutilation and operationalizing one-stop gender-based violence recovery centres in every county.

In July 2026, the Government of Kenya, through the State Department for Gender and Affirmative Action under the Ministry of Gender, Culture and Children Services and partners convened a national consultative forum on the implementation of the recommendations and sustainability.

"The Ministry of Health remains committed to strengthening the health sector's role in preventing and responding to gender-based violence. Our priority is to ensure that women and girls can access timely, quality and survivor-centred services, while strengthening prevention, early identification, referral and coordination across the health system and with other sectors," says Mary Gathitu, Sexual and Reproductive Health and Rights Programme Lead at Kenya's Ministry of Health. "Ultimately, protecting women and girls from violence requires sustained, coordinated action at both national and county levels."

World Health Organization (WHO) has supported Ministry of Health to conduct assessments of health facility readiness to respond to gender-based violence cases in six counties and has trained more than 250 health workers on the clinical management of gender-based violence survivors since 2025. The Organization also sits on the technical working group that provides support to Ministry of Health on gender-based violence interventions.

“Gender-based violence, particularly intimate partner and sexual violence, is a major public health and human rights concern, rooted in unequal gender norms and power dynamics," says Dr. Rita Arogo, Maternal and Reproductive Health Officer at WHO Kenya. "Its prevention and elimination must be elevated as a priority for action and advocacy at the highest levels."

item.title: Ethiopia launches polio vaccination campaign to protect more than 11 million children: WHO deployed 28 staff to support the vaccination campaign
item.description:
Country: Ethiopia
Source: World Health Organization

Addis Ababa, Ethiopia, 21 November 2026 – The Government of Ethiopia, in collaboration with the World Health Organization (WHO), UNICEF, the Global Polio Eradication Initiative (GPEI) partners, and other partners, launched a polio vaccination campaign aimed at protecting more than 11.3 million children from poliovirus infection. The polio vaccination campaign, which is launched today, 21 November 2026 will be implemented across five regions including Addis Ababa, Oromia, Central Ethiopia, South Ethiopia and Southwest Ethiopia. Speaking on the launch of the polio vaccination held today in Arba Minch, South Ethiopia Region, Dr Loveday Nkwogu who delivered the partner’s joint speech on behalf of Prof. Francis Kasolo, WHO Representative to Ethiopia, emphasized the importance of collective action to protect children from polio.

"Every child vaccinated during this vaccination campaign brings Ethiopia to contributing one step closer to a polio-free future. While significant progress has been made, poliovirus continues to threaten children wherever immunity gaps exist. We call on parents, community leaders, health workers and partners to join forces to ensure that every eligible child is reached, protected and given a healthy start in life."

WHO has deployed 28 it’s central and field staff to support this vaccination campaign. WHO’s technical team have been supporting key activities to ensure that all eligible children are reached during the vaccination campaign including coordination, advocacy, microplanning, Training of health workers at national and regional level, training of supervisors for the Open Data Kit (ODK) utilization, as well as for Independent monitors and lot quality assurance sampling (LQAS) surveyors to be deployed during and after the vaccination campaign to ensure its quality, to support supervision on the campaign implementation, data management, and community engagement to ensure the quality of the vaccination campaign.

The first round of the vaccination campaign will be conducted from 21-24 November 2026, followed by a second round from 18-21 December 2026. During the vaccination campaign, a vaccination team composed of health workers and community volunteers will conduct a house-to-house visits to vaccinate every eligible child in the household with life-saving polio vaccine to protect against polio.

In addition to administering polio vaccines, the vaccination teams will identify zero-dose and under-vaccinated children during the house-to-house visits and link them with routine immunization services to ensure they receive the missed routine vaccines.

Although Ethiopia remains free of wild poliovirus, outbreaks of circulating variant poliovirus continue to pose a threat, particularly in areas with immunity gaps and high population movement. This year, cases of circulating variant poliovirus type 1 were reported from Gambella, Oromia and South Ethiopia regions, underscoring the need for rapid and high-quality vaccination responses to protect children and stop transmission. Similar polio vaccination campaigns have been already conducted in Gambella and Benishangul Gumuz Region and two Zones of Oromia Region (West Wolleag and Kelm Wollega).

The current polio vaccination campaign builds on the success of previous outbreak response efforts conducted in Gambella, Benishangul-Gumuz and parts of Oromia region, which reached more than 1 million children and demonstrated the effectiveness of coordinated action among government authorities, communities, health workers and partners.

WHO and partners are also calling for increasing efforts to strengthen vaccine preventable surveillance alongside with vaccination efforts. High-quality Acute Flaccid Paralysis (AFP) and environmental surveillance remain essential to rapidly detect and respond to any poliovirus transmission and safeguard the gains achieved in polio eradication efforts.

The World Health Organization continues to provide technical and operational support to the Government of Ethiopia, including during planning, coordination, monitoring, supervision and surveillance activities, as part of the global effort to eradicate polio once and for all.

Ethiopia joins the global community in reaffirming its commitment to ensuring that no child is missed, no community is left behind, and every child is protected from vaccine-preventable diseases.

item.title: UNHCR Ecuador - Operational Update No. 10 | October 2026
item.description:
Countries: Ecuador, Colombia, Venezuela (Bolivarian Republic of)
Source: UN High Commissioner for Refugees

Please refer to the attached file.

Operational context

Ecuador continued to face a complex security crisis linked to organized criminal groups across several provinces. In response to increased violence, the Government introduced a new nighttime curfew in Guayas, Manabí, Los Ríos, El Oro and Esmeraldas in early November. Security concerns also persisted along the northern border. In Sucumbíos and Carchi, the presence of Colombian non-state armed groups and illegal economies continued to affect remote areas and Indigenous territories. These volatile conditions, together with mobility restrictions associated with security measures, added operational and access challenges hindering refugees, asylum-seekers and host communities from accessing essential services.

Heavy rainfall associated with the 2026–2027 El Niño phenomenon intensified during October, affecting communities across the country, particularly in coastal regions. According to Ecuador’s National Secretariat for Risk Management, 57,625 people were impacted, including 43,125 affected, 12 casualties reported and more than 13,700 homes had sustained damage across 23 provinces. Esmeraldas, Guayas, El Oro, Los Ríos and Manabí, all refugee hosting areas, were among the provinces reporting the greatest impact, alongside Bolívar, Azuay and Santo Domingo de los Tsáchilas. October accounted for the highest frequency of events during the reporting period, reinforcing concerns over further flooding, disaster-related displacements and disruptions to services in affected communities. UNHCR continued coordinating with national and local authorities and partners to identify refugees and other forcibly displaced people affected by these incidents and facilitate their inclusion in existing assessment and response mechanisms.

Energy supply remained under pressure as prolonged dry conditions in the highlands affected water levels at hydroelectric reservoirs, despite heavy rainfall in other parts of the country. The Government introduced measures to reduce electricity demand among high-voltage users, while Ecuador continued importing electricity from Colombia to support national generation capacity. Some areas experienced unplanned outages, affecting households, businesses and productive activities. Recent rainfall contributed to a partial recovery of the Mazar reservoir, although energy availability requires close monitoring. The combination of security incidents, severe weather and disruptions to infrastructure and services continued to shape the operating environment, requiring close coordination with authorities and partners to safeguard protection and service delivery.

UNHCR continues working closely with national and local authorities, partners and communities to monitor the evolving context and its impact on refugees and host communities. UNHCR focuses on strengthening preparedness and coordination to respond to sudden emergencies, securing uninterrupted access to protection and essential services, supporting government-led emergency response mechanisms to ensure the inclusion of forcibly displaced people, and adapting localized activities, including protection monitoring, in hard-to reach areas, while maintaining essential protection services.

item.description:
Countries: Ecuador, Colombia, Venezuela (Bolivarian Republic of)
Source: UN High Commissioner for Refugees

Please refer to the attached file.

Contexto operacional

Ecuador continuó enfrentando un complejo contexto de seguridad debido a la presencia de grupos de delincuencia organizada en varias provincias. Ante el incremento de la violencia, el Gobierno anunció un nuevo toque de queda nocturno en Guayas, Manabí, Los Ríos, El Oro y Esmeraldas, previsto para los primeros días de noviembre. En la frontera norte, la presencia de grupos armados no estatales colombianos y economías ilegales continuó afectando a zonas remotas y territorios indígenas de Sucumbíos y Carchi. Estas condiciones volátiles y las restricciones de movilidad asociadas a las medidas de seguridad generaron desafíos operativos y limitaron el acceso a servicios esenciales para personas refugiadas, solicitantes de asilo y comunidades de acogida.

Las fuertes lluvias asociadas al fenómeno de El Niño 2026- 2027 se intensificaron durante octubre, especialmente en regiones de la Costa. Según la Secretaría Nacional de Gestión de Riesgos, 57.625 personas resultaron impactadas, incluidas 43.125 personas afectadas. Además, se reportaron 12 fallecimientos y más de 13.700 viviendas sufrieron daños en 23 provincias. Esmeraldas, Guayas, El Oro, Los Ríos y Manabí, todas con personas refugiadas, registraron algunos de los mayores impactos, junto con Bolívar, Azuay y Santo Domingo de los Tsáchilas. Octubre concentró la mayor frecuencia de eventos del período, aumentando la preocupación ante nuevas inundaciones, desplazamientos generados por desastres e interrupciones de servicios. ACNUR coordinó con autoridades y socios para identificar a personas refugiadas y otras personas en situación de desplazamiento forzado afectadas, y facilitar su inclusión en los mecanismos existentes de evaluación y respuesta.

El suministro eléctrico permaneció bajo presión debido a la prolongada sequía en la Sierra, que afectó los niveles de agua de los embalses hidroeléctricos, pese a las fuertes lluvias registradas en otras zonas. El Gobierno adoptó medidas para reducir la demanda de los usuarios de alto voltaje, mientras Ecuador continuó importando electricidad de Colombia para respaldar la generación nacional. Los cortes no programados afectaron a hogares, negocios y actividades productivas. Aunque las lluvias recientes contribuyeron a una recuperación parcial del embalse de Mazar, la disponibilidad energética requiere seguimiento. La combinación de incidentes de seguridad, eventos climáticos severos e interrupciones de infraestructura y servicios siguió condicionando el entorno operativo y el acceso a servicios esenciales. Ello requiere de seguimiento cercano con autoridades y socios para preservar la protección y el acceso a los servicios.

En este contexto, ACNUR sigue coordinando con autoridades, socios y comunidades para monitorear la evolución del contexto y sus efectos en las personas refugiadas y comunidades de acogida. La respuesta de ACNUR prioriza el fortalecimiento de la preparación y la coordinación para responder a emergencias súbitas, asegurando el acceso ininterrumpido a servicios de protección y esenciales, apoyando la inclusión de las personas afectadas en los mecanismos de respuesta a emergencias liderados por el Gobierno y la adaptación de actividades localizadas en zonas con restricciones de acceso, manteniendo los servicios de protección esenciales.

item.title: Defense Business Brief: Building warships; Drones; Neighborhood watch; and more...
How DARPA Challenged Teams to Bring Robots Into Disaster Triage
item.description:
On 5 November, 10 teams descended upon a 52-acre mock town in College Station, Texas called Disaster City. They were there for a nine-day competition to see how well teams of robots and humans could navigate simulated catastrophes, like a market ravaged by a tornado and a nighttime strike on a military base. At stake? US $2.5 million in prize money.

The scenarios were the final of the DARPA Triage Challenge, which the U.S. agency has been running for three years with the goal of saving more lives in urgent mass casualty events. Engineers from academia and industry have competed in elaborately staged mass casualty events, such as simulated combat zones and plane crash scenes. Teams spent years designing systems where autonomous ground robots and drones could help first responders find mock victims and decide the best way to care for them. “Triage is all about resources,” says Jeremy Pamplin, who managed the challenge for DARPA. Pamplin is a critical care physician and retired colonel who spent 28 years in the U.S. Army.

In mass casualty events, medics race to assess trauma with finite resources and limited time. Some victims need urgent help that medics can provide immediately, like tourniquets to halt bleeding. Some need evacuation and surgery. Others don’t need immediate help—either because their wounds are minimal enough, or because they’re so severe that a medic’s attention is better served elsewhere. Medics must prioritize who gets what care, but the line between each of these scenarios can be murky amid the rubble, frenzy, and heat of the moment.

It’s a difficult problem, and so the technologies developed in this competition could help real-world decisionmaking, says Gabriela Garcia Dolagaray, assistant medical director for emergency preparedness at Massachusetts General Hospital and the Brigham and Women’s Hospital in Boston. “Finding people can sometimes just be dangerous,” she says, “and getting a robust number of people to go out and search in a disaster area will take time.”

Trauma Technologies and the DARPA Triage Challenge

The Triage Challenge is the latest in a long DARPA legacy of running grand challenges to incentivize proof-of-concept development of important technologies. This particular challenge began as a program to quickly detect signs of trauma. DARPA imagined not only that drones and robots could find casualties, but that machine learning algorithms could assist in triage—which, at its core, is the process of assessing injuries and prioritizing care in a medical emergency.

Pamplin took over the competition in May 2025. “I have friends that still wake up in the middle of the night with these types of recollections and wondering if they did the right thing in the moment during a mass casualty incident,” Pamplin says. “That moves me. I would very much like to eliminate that uncertainty for them to the extent possible with this type of technology.”

He used his experience to make the competition increasingly elaborate and realistic. Year one featured a simulated convoy attack, and human participants sat in protective enclosures to avoid incidental run-ins with robots. In year two, when Pamplin took over the challenge, his team incorporated a full-size airplane fuselage to simulate a plane crash with dozens of victims. Organizers learned to recreate the physical environment of a disaster, and also the physical signs of injuries, like warm blood. Pamplin’s team visited a slaughterhouse with thermal cameras to study the temperature of blood spilling onto the ground. In the competition, they mimic that effect by heating water in a coffee pot and pouring it beside the body. This lets teams detect bleeding even at night.

A man performs a simulated triage as part of DARPA’s Triage Challenge finals. The program was designed to see how robots could assist in making triage decisions during an emergency.Paul Flacks/DARPA

“They always are throwing additional challenging things at us that you wouldn’t expect,” says Sam Colachis, a biomedical engineer at Battelle, an applied science and technology nonprofit in Columbus Ohio who led the organization’s DART team—short for “Drone-Assisted Rapid Triage”—in the competition.

The tactics required for successful triage are inherently multidisciplinary, says Derek Paley, a professor of aerospace engineering leading the University of Maryland’s team, RoboScout. Before 2022, Paley felt confident in his lab’s skills with autonomous navigation and algorithms, but he knew little about trauma medicine. “I didn’t even know what triage was,” he says.

Paley recruited colleagues in emergency medicine to help design his team’s approach and shape their tech. Before the Triage Challenge began, they felt like an underdog. “We kind of have a chip on our shoulder because we think we can play on the same field as these other teams…who’ve done grand challenges before,” Paley told Spectrum before the competition. They finished third in the first year of competition and second last year.

Each year’s competition began with four smaller trials that tested specific components of a robotic system. Teams first released their robots to locate as many casualties (a mix of live actors and manikins) as possible in 15 minutes. Next, they spent five minutes triaging injuries. Another trial presented teams with a fixed number of casualties in known locations to test how they assess trauma. Then, teams had ten minutes to collect vitals like pulse and breathing rate remotely from a few meters away. The top four teams moved into a semi-final where their robots worked with two human medics in simulated emergencies. And the two teams who performed best in four human-machine runs then moved to a 25-minute championship run.

Robots, Drones, and Autonomous Triage

When the teams arrived at Disaster City, they knew very little about the details of what awaited them. One self-funded team of college students from Delhi Technological University flew from India with 22 checked bags, each containing disembodied drones and wheeled robots they had handbuilt. Their team, Unmanned Aerial Systems, learned in the two prior years of the contest to simply expect the unexpected—from DARPA and their own systems. Upon arrival this year, they unzipped their luggage to find broken motors and chassis, camera parts, and missing screws. “We’re still trying to assemble everything before the competition,” Nishant Chandna calmly told IEEE Spectrum a couple days before the challenge. “It’s just part of it.”

Most teams in the challenge designed systems with a mix of ground robots and aerial drones. The student team from India built drones and wheeled robots to search for mock victims with onboard cameras and lidar.

But wheeled robots are problematic. They are more stable, cheaper, and easier to control than legged robots, but they struggle with stairs, entryways, and rough terrain littered with rubble. “We really needed a platform that could traverse those obstacles pretty easily,” says Eric Eaton, a machine learning scientist who led the University of Pennsylvania’s team, which began with drones and wheeled robots before expanding their fleet with four-legged Spot robots from Boston Dynamics that make it up stairs.

Paley’s RoboScout team opted for a strategy that involved sensing the scene from the ground. Their “dogs,” which were also Spot robots, listen for screaming victims, and help in one of the most difficult challenges in autonomous triage: quickly sensing vitals from with thermal cameras and radar. Millimeter-wave radar can detect the subtle movement of a pulse, and thermal cameras can measure breathing rates based on how breathing changes the temperature around a mouth and nose.

Battelle’s team had relied entirely on drones, even for measuring vital signs. Colachis says his team fuses inputs from multiple sensors including thermal, radar, and visual to calculate vitals. The team became almost notorious for their commitment to drones. “They keep threatening to bring a ground robot,” says RoboScout’s Paley, “but they always show up with drones.” For the first two years of the competition, it worked—Battelle won the first two rounds of the competition.

Members of the University of Maryland’s RoboScout team (on right) celebrate a successful run during the DARPA Triage Challenge finals.Paul Flacks/DARPA

RoboScout Wins DARPA Triage Grand Prize

During the final, organizers cast more than 500 actors to simulate casualties throughout the week. DARPA chose these actors to make obstacles like sensing vitals more realistic than previous years. Some were college students instructed to increase their heart and breathing rate on exercise bikes to simulate shock. Endurance athletes were instructed to lower their heart rates, simulating other injuries like airway failures. In the military base simulation, soldiers were running around a compound with alarms blaring. “Some of the explosions caused some of the medics to actually react to it,” Pamplin says, and “pull people to the ground so they didn’t get hit.”

Battelle did finally show up with a ground robot to help with measuring vitals remotely. But this time, the twice-champ finished second. The winner of DARPA’s Triage Challenge grand prize was the RoboScout team from the University of Maryland. The grand prize earned them $1.5 million.

After a perilous start slowed by software errors relating to the competition’s timer and Wi-Fi RoboScout rallied back through the final human-machine teaming portion. “We got hot at the right time,” Paley says. “It was pretty surreal.”

Other teams performed well despite having to improvise through engineering hiccups. Carnegie Mellon’s team, Chiron, struggled with a GPS error. After fixing it, they raced back and nearly made the final. The student team from Delhi didn’t meet a threshold for autonomous control in the competition, but they did earn the highest score in one sub-competition, winning $300,000.

“It’s an incredibly exciting challenge,” says Peter Fischer, trauma medical director with Washington Regional Medical Center in Fayetteville, Arkansas. “We struggle, especially with mass casualty incidents, in determining who the sickest patients are. In trauma, especially, you have to make sure that you triage these patients appropriately, so the sickest ones not only get the care the fastest, but get to the right place at the right time.”

Fischer was intrigued by a non-robotic branch of the competition, where two new teams excelled in predicting urgent care with the help of AI agents. He imagines these advances in robotics and algorithms could connect with additional data from hospitals. Triage algorithms could suggest where to take them to avoid overloading specific hospitals, he says, “That’s where we can really start to make a big difference.”

Although the competition has ended, the work continues. Several participants told IEEE Spectrum they plan to bring their teams’ AI algorithms elsewhere, such as hospital trauma bays, regional medical emergencies, and chemical weapon response.

For his part, DARPA’s Pamplin was most eager to compare performance to human medics without robots. A human-only team located 50 percent of casualties on average in daytime simulations; when paired with medics on one run of the same course, Maryland’s robots found every one. “That was the first time we’ve ever seen that,” he says. In the championship run, humans provided life-saving interventions to 25 percent of the mock casualties who needed them—RoboScout treated 74 percent. “That’s a couple lives,” Pamplin says. “That’s a couple humans that didn’t die that day.”
